Galore means in large, plentiful, often impressive quantities. When something exists galore, there is a lot of it — more than enough, an abundance of it. Think of it as a stronger, more vivid way of saying "plenty of" or "lots and lots of."
The One Rule That Makes "Galore" Unique

Here is the single most important thing to know about this word, and it is what makes it special among English adjectives:

"Galore" always comes after the noun it describes — never before it.

Most adjectives in English come before the noun:

a beautiful garden, a long road, many books

But "galore" breaks this rule completely. It follows the noun, every single time:

✅ "There were bargains galore at the market."
❌ "There were galore bargains at the market." (This is wrong.)

This placement after the noun is called being postpositive, and galore is one of the very few common English adjectives that works this way. If you place it before the noun, native speakers will immediately know something is off.

There is also a second rule: you cannot use "galore" after a linking verb like is, was, are, were, or seems:

❌ "The bargains were galore." (This is wrong.)
✅ "There were bargains galore." (This is right.)

So the only correct pattern is: [Noun] + galore. That's it.
What It Feels Like to Use This Word

"Galore" is not a neutral, dry word. It carries a sense of enthusiasm, emphasis, or delight — as if the speaker is almost amazed or pleased by the abundance. It often makes a sentence feel lively and expressive.

Compare these two sentences:

"There were a lot of options at the store."
"There were options galore at the store."

Both sentences say roughly the same thing, but the second one sounds more vivid and enthusiastic. It paints a more colorful picture.
It Can Be Used in Both Positive and Negative Situations

Galore simply describes a large quantity. The context of the sentence, not the word itself, tells you whether that abundance is a good thing or a bad thing.

Positive:

"The festival had music, food, and entertainment galore." (Lucky! What a great festival.)
"She had opportunities galore in her new job." (Very fortunate.)
"On her birthday, there were gifts galore under the tree." (How wonderful.)

Negative:

"After the storm, there were problems galore." (Unfortunately, so many problems.)
"The report was full of errors galore." (So many mistakes — not good.)
"The renovation caused delays galore." (Frustratingly many delays.)

As you can see, "galore" itself is not positive or negative. It simply intensifies the quantity of whatever noun it follows.

"Galore" does not mean a specific number. It means abundantly many — enough that the quantity is striking or noteworthy. Think of it as crossing a threshold where the amount is no longer ordinary. It is not just "some" or even just "many" — it is an impressive, standout abundance.
Register: When Do People Use This Word?

"Galore" is an informal to semi-formal word. You will find it in:

  • Everyday conversation
  • Newspaper headlines and magazine articles
  • Advertising ("Deals galore this weekend!")
  • Stories and creative writing

It is not typically used in very formal academic or legal writing, where neutral words like "an abundance of" or "numerous" would be preferred instead.

FeatureDetail
  • Meaning: in large, impressive, plentiful supply
  • Position: always after the noun — never before it, never after a linking verb
  • Tone: enthusiastic, vivid, expressive
  • Polarity: neutral — works in both happy and unhappy situations
  • Register: informal to semi-formal

One final example to lock it in:
"At the end-of-year sale, there were discounts galore, crowds galore, and noise galore — but bargains galore too."

That single sentence shows you the word used four times in a row, all correctly placed after each noun, and covering both positive (discounts, bargains) and negative (crowds, noise) contexts.
